transcript.text: Right, Lucy, Karim, tell me about your visitor survey at the City Museum.
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: It was a long project, but we really enjoyed it. The museum staff were very friendly and gave us a quiet room for the interviews.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: Good. A supportive environment makes a big difference to the quality of the data.
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: We interviewed visitors on four Saturdays in March. In total we spoke to a hundred and twenty people.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: Most of them were local residents, which surprised us, because we had assumed tourists would dominate.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: Did you notice any differences between the visitors who came alone and those who came in groups?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: Yes, people in groups spent more time in the gift shop, but those alone stayed longer in the galleries.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: What was the main reason for visiting?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: The temporary exhibition on ancient jewellery. Seventy percent mentioned it first.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: People also liked the free entry. When we asked what would stop them returning, the most common answer was the café prices.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: Food and drink prices are always a popular complaint. Did the museum respond when you mentioned it?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: The manager said she would look into it, but she couldn't promise anything.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: Did you ask about opening hours?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: Yes, many working people want evening opening on Thursdays, until nine o'clock.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: And younger visitors asked for more interactive displays, particularly touch screens.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: Those are useful findings. Did you compare your results with the national figures?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: We tried, but the national survey is quite old, so we only used it as background information.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: How will you present the data?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: We thought of a poster, but then we realised a short film with quotes from visitors would be more engaging.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: A film takes time. Do you have the equipment?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: The media department lends cameras, but only to third-year students, and we're in second year.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: We did ask once, but they said the cameras are booked months in advance.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: Then borrow a phone. Quality is good enough nowadays. What worries you most?
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: Permission. We need visitors to sign consent forms if they're filmed.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: Use the university's standard form; it's on the ethics page.
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: We were going to write our own, so thanks.
transcript.speaker: KARIM

transcript.text: We'll also give the participants a copy of the film afterwards, as a thank-you.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: That's a nice gesture. It also helps the museum feel involved in the project.
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: Last thing: the assessment. Fifty percent is for content, thirty for presentation and twenty for teamwork.
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: Thanks, that's helpful.
transcript.speaker: LUCY

transcript.text: I'm looking forward to seeing the film. Send me an outline by next week.
transcript.speaker: MR ADAMS

transcript.text: Will do, thank you.
transcript.speaker: KARIM
